ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Sample Selection Methods on Real-World Noisy Label Datasets
PROPOSAL: Compare state-of-the-art sample selection methods (Co-teaching, MentorNet, SMOTE) on several popular real-world noisy label benchmark datasets (Section 4 of the paper "learning from noisy labels: A Survey" by Zhang et al.) using accuracy and true positive rate (APR) as evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: 
- Train a baseline model (ResNet-18) with clean labels on each dataset.
- Evaluate the same models with all methods turned off, i.e., training on the original noisy labels without any sample selection or correction.
- Compare different sample selection method variants with default hyperparameters.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results: MentorNet could outperform Co-teaching due to its built-in teacher-student mechanism, and model accuracy would strongly correlate with the level of noise in each dataset. Failure might come from the fact that some methods might over-correct, excluding valuable correct labels as well, leading to performance degradation.

The next proposal will consider label correction strategies that aren't based on cross-validation or sampling statistics but rather on direct exploration of label possibilities.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Exposing and Quantifying Label Noise in Instance-Dependent Scenarios
PROPOSAL: Develop an instance-dependent (ID) noise characterization framework using gradient-based and adversarial-based methods (Gradient-based methods use a model's output by looking at how model decisions change when samples are perturbed, while adversarial methods use the model's prediction loss to identify if-example patterns). Utilize the Caltech-101 and CIFAR-100 datasets, which are known to have instance-dependent label noise, to quantify the nature and level of this noise.
CONTROLS: Use a subset of instances with clean labels as ground truth for noise characterization. Evaluate the ID noise characterization framework using precision and recall as evaluation metrics, plus a permutation test to assess the ID signal in the noise patterns.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results: The framework would expose the existence of instance-dependent noise, establish its impact on model generalization, and demonstrate useful insights into the structure of this noise. Failure might come from the difficulty in consistently identifying precise noise sources with this quantitative approach in the complex instance-dependent scenarios.

The next proposal or revision will consider augmenting the existing label correction methods with model effectiveness assessments.

Use the gradients of loss function and learned representations of different models to expose whether sample selection methods are, in practice, picking up real underlying patterns in the data, or merely exploiting the characteristics of the training mechanism.
CONTROLS: Compare the same baseline and "noisy labels" controls from the original proposal, with an added experiment that uses the ID noise characterization framework to refine and test the self-purification dynamics of sample selection methods.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (5 additional hours for the newly characterized and tested sample selection methods)
PREDICTION: Expected results: This integration would add value to proposal 1 by providing insights into the dynamics of label noise correction as associated with certain selections and, further, should show which specific instances of noisy labels are being identified and selected by sample selection methods and under what conditions (e.g. region-based class conditional noise). Failure might occur if this integration causes resource constraints.

Moving forward, this next proposal will build from the noisy label quantification approach and supervised learning, by taking a step back and exploring theoretical aspects of noisy label learning.

Next proposal: With the theoretical framework in place, a follow-up experiment using semi-supervised learning will introduce new insights into effects that instance-dependent noise may have on multitask label exploration.

TITLE: Meta-Learning for Adaptive Noisy Label Correction
PROPOSAL: Design a meta-learning framework that can learn to correct noisy labels adaptively based on the instance-dependent noise patterns learned during the meta-training phase. Utilize a few-shot learning approach to adapt the learned noise correction rules to new, unseen datasets with different types of instance-dependent noise.

PROPOSAL: Perform a longitudinal study to examine the effects of instance-dependent noise on the performance of classification models over an extended period, focusing on the model's ability to learn and adapt to evolving datasets with changing noise patterns. Utilize a real-world dataset with a large number of instances and multiple assessment points over several months.

The final proposal will explore the intersection of explainability and noisy labels, aiming to develop techniques for understanding and visualizing the impact of instance-dependent noise on model predictions.

TITLE: Robust Label Correction via Stochastic Optimization
PROPOSAL: We propose to adopt a stochastic optimization framework, specifically Adam, to iteratively correct and refine noisy labels, with candidates selected based on their uncertainty and influence on re-averaging the noisy label. Specifically, an instance is selected from the noisy dataset based on a sampled baseline model's uncertainty or prediction loss. Its potentially mislabeled instance is then reweighted towards a prediction generated by a more accurate, regularized, model trained on clean labels, the updated instance being considered as its new candidate noisy label. Notably, this gradual refinement approach of multiple iterations encourages continued adaptation to noisy input, by concentric contraction of the updated set of candidate noisy labels, in relation to what would have been expected by a given level of model confidence.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard model training; Baseline 2: robust regularization of the original model; others: variants such as reverse 2-stage correction methods, standard or momentum stochastic optimization and swapping of the training set with noisy noised weak targets; Baseline 3: set where each of the noisy training labels is replaced by its average of all possible clean labels.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should improve robustness to instance-dependent label-noise over the baselines, but we anticipate performance degradation where noise distributions are irregular.

TITLE: Leveraging Knowledge Distillation for Noisy Label Correction
PROPOSAL: We propose a knowledge distillation framework to leverage teacher models trained on noisy labels, aiming to alleviate the noise effects and refine the noisy labels. Specifically, we employ a student model to learn from multiple teacher models that are trained on the noisy dataset with different levels of regularization, and combine the predictions from these teacher models using an ensemble-based approach.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard training with noisy labels; Baseline 2: teacher-student (T-S) training with a single teacher; Baseline 3: gradient-based label correction (refactored).

We also introduce a regularization term to encourage the student model to produce coherent and confident predictions.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should leverage the strengths of multiple teacher models and improve the robustness against noisy labels, however, it might be computationally intensive and sensitive to the choice of teacher models and regularization weights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning with Noisy Label Correction for Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel transfer learning approach for domain adaptation with noisy labels, aiming to adapt a pre-trained model to a new domain with noisy labels. Specifically, we integrate the robust label correction methods from previous experiments into a domain adaptation framework, which involves three stages: 1) learning a pre-trained model on a source domain with a small amount of noisy labels; 2) correcting the noisy labels in the source domain using the proposed robust label correction methods; 3) fine-tuning the corrected model on the target domain.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: domain adaptation without noisy label correction; Baseline 2: transfer learning with domain adaptation; Baseline 3: robust regularization of the original model; Baseline 4: combination of robust regularization and domain adaptation.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should improve the adaptation performance of pre-trained models to new domains with noisy labels, but might require careful tuning of hyperparameters and domain adaptation techniques to achieve robust results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Noise-Aware Early Stopping for Noisy Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose a noise-aware early stopping criterion for noisy classification tasks, aiming to detect overfitting to noisy labels and stop training before model performance degrades. Specifically, we track the model's performance on clean labels (detected using a confidence threshold or clustering) and stop training when the performance on clean labels starts to degrade, indicating that the model has begun to overfit to noisy labels.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard early stopping criteria based on validation accuracy; Baseline 2: robust regularization of the original model; Baseline 3: combination of robust regularization and noise-aware early stopping.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should help prevent overfitting to noisy labels and improve the robustness of models to noise, but might require careful tuning of the confidence threshold or clustering parameters to achieve good results.

ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Noise-Aware Early Stopping for Noisy Classification
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive noise-aware early stopping criterion that dynamically adjusts the confidence threshold and clustering parameters based on the model's performance on a validation set with clean labels. Specifically, we use a nested loop approach, where the outer loop optimizes the confidence threshold and clustering parameters based on the performance of the model on a validation set, and the inner loop optimizes the model parameters given the best-performing threshold and clustering parameters found so far.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard early stopping criteria based on validation accuracy; Baseline 2: robust regularization of the original model; Baseline 3: combination of robust regularization and noise-aware early stopping with a fixed confidence threshold and clustering parameters.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should improve the robustness of models to noise and prevent overfitting to noisy labels, but might require careful tuning of the optimization parameters and the adaptation rate of the confidence threshold and clustering parameters to achieve good results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Objective Optimization for Noisy Label Correction and Regularization
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-objective optimization framework for noisy label correction and regularization, aiming to optimize both the accuracy of the model on clean labels and its robustness to noisy labels. Specifically, we use a co-evolutionary algorithm to optimize two objectives: the accuracy on clean labels and a regularization term that encourages the model to be robust to noisy labels.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: standard multi-objective optimization; Baseline 2: single-objective optimization with the accuracy on clean labels; Baseline 3: single-objective optimization with the robustness to noisy labels; Baseline 4: combination of robust regularization and noise-aware early stopping.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method should improve both the accuracy and robustness of models to noise, but might be computationally intensive due to the complexity of the multi-objective optimization problem.

TITLE: Instance-dependent label noise correction via probabilistic label refinement
PROPOSAL: We propose a method that learns to correct noisy labels by iteratively refining the probabilities of each label, conditioning on the model's past prediction losses and confidence levels. This approach is based on a probabilistic refinement module that combines instance-dependent corruption probabilities and instance features to predict the probability of the true label.
CONTROLS: We compare our method to several state-of-the-art noisy label correction methods, including the popular Co-teaching and Mentornet algorithms. We also perform ablations to evaluate the importance of each refinement step and the impact of varying corruption probability budgets. 
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method should outperform Co-teaching and Mentornet on several real-world datasets with instance-dependent label noise, such as ImageNet-C and CIFAR-100. It may struggle to achieve high correction accuracy in highly noisy regimes where corruption probabilities are very close to 1.

TITLE: Semi-supervised learning framework for noisy label correction
PROPOSAL: We extend the probabilistic label refinement module from proposal 1 to propose a semi-supervised framework (SSL-NLC) that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to correct noisy labels. The framework uses a jointly trained classification and denoising module where the classification module is used to predict class probabilities and the denoising module is used to predict the likelihood of each data point being noisy.
CONTROLS: We compare SSL-NLC with its fully supervised variant (from proposal 1), self-training based baseline (where unlabeled samples are added as labeled during training), and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning algorithms such as Mean Teacher and MixMatch. 
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: SSL-NLC should improve label correction accuracy especially in cases where the unlabeled data provides valuable information about the true labels. It may struggle with adaptation to new unseen classes.
